title: Pick the move order for the structure you want
outcomes: Chooses between two move orders by the structure wanted and predicts the structure each leads to
Checks what the opponent's last move attacks before aiming at a structure
Recognises positions where no move order is yet choosing a structure

steps.text: In **Name the structure whatever the move order** you read structures from the pawns. Now you *choose*. A move order can let your opponent steer elsewhere. Test each early move: what does it make playable for me, and what does it allow? Example: the Maroczy bind, White pawns on c4 and e4 with no d-pawn.

steps.caption: Black's 4th move g6, then the bind: 1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4.

line.say: White builds the second pawn; nothing attacks e4.
The bishop reaches the long diagonal.
White develops the bishop to a central square.
Black's knight now attacks e4; the knight on c3 comes next to guard it.
Black's d-pawn steps up; the bind stays.

claims.statement: At the end White has a pawn on c4.
White has no d-pawn and Black has no c-pawn.

steps.title: Same wish, three move orders
steps.prompt: White wants pawns on c4 and e4. Predict what each position allows, then check.

steps.text: **When a move order works.** The wish alone does not decide; the last move does. After 4...Nf6 the pawn on e4 is attacked, so the wish fails; after 4...g6 it works; and which pawn moves first (c4 or e4) does not matter. **Rule of thumb:** before you commit, check what your opponent's last move attacks. A prediction covers the line shown, not the game: the opponent can choose another order.

steps.prompt: Pick a line from your repertoire where two move orders reach different structures. Decide which order you want, with the checks that make it safe.
